The Darboux definitions [F4] give linearity: for integrable $u,w$, choose grid partitions whose upper-minus lower sums for each are arbitrarily small, take a common refinement, and use $\inf(u+w)\ge\inf u+\inf w$ and $\sup(u+w)\le\sup u+\sup w$ on each cell. The upper-minus-lower gap for $u+w$ is therefore bounded by the sum of the chosen gaps, so $u+w$ is integrable. Its lower and upper integrals are squeezed between the sums of the lower integrals of $u,w$ and the sums of their upper integrals; letting the gaps tend to zero gives $\int_Q(u+w)=\int_Qu+\int_Qw$. For a scalar $c>0$, upper and lower sums scale by $c$; for $c<0$ they exchange after scaling, giving $\int_Q(cu)=c\int_Qu$, and $c=0$ gives zero. Also, if $|u|\le\varepsilon$ on $Q$, each lower sum is at least $-\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ and each upper sum at most $\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$, since cell volumes add to $\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ by [F5]. Thus $|\int_\sigma u|\le\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ for an integrable function on the simplex bounded by $\varepsilon$. [F3, F4, F5]

Fix a parameter chart and a point $p$. For one simplex $\sigma$ write $\sigma^*\alpha_p=f(p,z)\,dz_1\wedge dz_2\wedge dz_3$ on $T_3$. Choose a closed parameter rectangle $R$ around $p$ inside the chart. The displayed inequalities defining $T_3$ make it closed and bounded, hence compact by [F6]; [F2] identifies it as the integration domain. The product $R\times T_3$ is a closed bounded Euclidean set, hence compact by [F6], so $\partial_a f$ is uniformly continuous there by [F7]. For a small nonzero increment $h$ in coordinate $p^a$, [F8] gives $$\frac{f(p+he_a,z)-f(p,z)}{h}-\partial_af(p,z) =\frac1h\int_0^h\bigl(\partial_af(p+se_a,z)-\partial_af(p,z)\bigr)\,ds.$$ Uniform continuity makes the right side tend uniformly to zero on $T_3$ as $h\to0$. By step 1.1, the integral of this error tends to zero. Linearity therefore gives $$\partial_a\int_\sigma f(p,z)\,dz=\int_\sigma\partial_af(p,z)\,dz.$$ Applying the same argument to every parameter derivative of $f$ proves that all parameter partial derivatives of the simplex integral exist and are integrals of the corresponding derivatives. They are continuous: on a compact parameter rectangle, uniform continuity of each next derivative and step 1.1 bound the change in its integral by the uniform coefficient change times $\operatorname{vol}(Q)$. Hence this simplex integral is smooth. [F2, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1]

By [F1], $\Sigma$ is a finite linear combination of such simplices. Linearity from step 1.1 makes $I$ the corresponding finite linear combination of their smooth integrals and gives the asserted derivative formula for every parameter coordinate. Linearity in the tangent vector then gives the formula for every $v\in T_pP$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

Put $w=u-v$ and $F=F_u-F_v$. Subtracting the two equations and adding and subtracting each coefficient evaluated at $u$ gives $A^0(u)\partial_tw+\sum_iA^i(u)\partial_iw=F+Q$, where $Q=-(A^0(u)-A^0(v))\partial_tv-\sum_i(A^i(u)-A^i(v))\partial_iv-B(u)+B(v)$. This is an identity: the coefficient-difference terms multiplying derivatives of $v$ and the difference of the zero-order terms are exactly the residual after the common principal operator is applied to $w$. [given, F1, algebra]

The composition-difference estimates in [F3], the state bound $\|v\|_{L^\infty H^s}\le R_z$, and the time-derivative bound $\|\partial_tv\|_{L^\infty H^r}\le R_t$ from [F1] imply $\|Q(t)\|_{H^r}\le C\|w(t)\|_{H^r}$. Solving the displayed difference equation for $\partial_tw$ with $(A^0(u))^{-1}$, whose operator norm is at most $a^{-1}$ by [F4], and using multiplier bounds at order $r-1$ from [F3] gives $\|\partial_tw(t)\|_{H^{r-1}}\le C(\|w(t)\|_{H^r}+\|F(t)\|_{H^{r-1}})$; here $\|\partial_iw\|_{H^{r-1}}\le\|w\|_{H^r}$. [step 1.2, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

Define $E(t)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}(D^\alpha w)^{\mathsf T}A^0(t,x,u)D^\alpha w\,dx$. Put $a=A^0(t,x,u)$, $a_i=A^i(t,x,u)$, $y_\alpha=D^\alpha w$, and $h=\partial_tw$. For $E_N:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}\int(P_Ny_\alpha)^{\mathsf T}a(P_Ny_\alpha)$, the finite Fourier sums $P_Nw$ are $C^1$ in time by classical regularity, and differentiation gives $E_N'=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}(2\langle P_ND^\alpha h,aP_Ny_\alpha\rangle+\langle P_Ny_\alpha,\partial_ta\,P_Ny_\alpha\rangle)$. The one-order tail estimate [F10] gives $P_Ny_\alpha\to y_\alpha$ uniformly in $L^2$, since $w$ is bounded in $H^{r+1}$. Self-adjointness changes the first pairing to $\langle D^\alpha h,P_N(aP_Ny_\alpha)\rangle$. The product $ay_\alpha$ is uniformly bounded in $H^1$ by the Leibniz rule and uniform $C^1$ bound on $a$, so $\|P_N(aP_Ny_\alpha)-ay_\alpha\|_2\le\|a\|_\infty\|P_Ny_\alpha-y_\alpha\|_2+\|(P_N-I)(ay_\alpha)\|_2\to0$ uniformly on $J$. Because $D^\alpha h$ is uniformly bounded in $L^2$, the first pairings converge in $L^1(J)$; the quadratic pairings converge uniformly since $\partial_ta$ is bounded. Thus $E_N\to E$ uniformly and $E_N'\to\mathcal G$ in $L^1$, where $\mathcal G=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}(2\langle D^\alpha h,ay_\alpha\rangle+\langle y_\alpha,\partial_ta\,y_\alpha\rangle)$. Passing to the limit in $E_N(t)-E_N(t')=\int_{t'}^tE_N'$ shows $E$ is absolutely continuous and $E'=\mathcal G$ almost everywhere. Differentiating the difference equation in space is an $L^2$ identity almost everywhere because $w\in L^\infty H^{r+1}$, $h\in L^\infty H^r$, and $F+Q\in L^\infty(J;H^r)$ by steps 1.2 and 2.1; periodicity gives no boundary term. [given, step 1.2, step 2.1, F1, F3, F10, algebra]

The derivatives of $A^\mu(t,x,u)$ are bounded on the fixed compact coefficient set. The $Q$ term is bounded by [step 2.1]; the commutator terms by [F3] and the $H^{r-1}$ bound on $\partial_tw$ from that step; and the forcing pairing $\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}\langle D^\alpha w,D^\alpha F\rangle$ by $\|w\|_{H^r}\|F\|_{H^r}$. Absorbing the quadratic lower-order terms with $2xy\le x^2+y^2$ while retaining the forcing pairing in mixed form, and using [F4] for energy equivalence, gives $E'(t)\le C E(t)+C\sqrt{E(t)}\|F(t)\|_{H^r}$ and $a\|w(t)\|_{H^r}^2\le E(t)\le b\|w(t)\|_{H^r}^2$ almost everywhere. The convergence established in step 3.1 justifies all time-derivative and commutator pairings. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F3, F4, F10, algebra]

For $\varepsilon>0$, set $Y_\varepsilon=(E+\varepsilon)^{1/2}$. Step 3.2 gives $Y_\varepsilon'\le (C/2)Y_\varepsilon+(C/2)\|F\|_{H^r}$, hence integration yields $Y_\varepsilon(t)\le e^{Ct/2}Y_\varepsilon(0)+(C/2)\int_0^t e^{C(t-r')/2}\|F(r')\|_{H^r}\,dr'$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using the energy equivalence of step 3.2 gives the stated estimate after enlarging $C$ to absorb $\sqrt{b/a}$ and $C/2$. When $F=0$, it is the homogeneous estimate. [step 3.2, F4, algebra]

Fix a smooth reference solution $\bar u$ with state range in $K_0$. Compactness gives a positive distance $d$ from its range to the complement of $\operatorname{int}K_1$. Put $\rho:=1+\|\bar u\|_{C(J;H^r)}$ and take initial data in an $H^s$ ball of radius at most $1$ about $\bar u(0)$, so their $H^s$ norms have a common bound $R_0:=1+\|\bar u(0)\|_{H^s}$. On any solution interval where $\|u-\bar u\|_{C(H^r)}<1$, the lower norm is at most $\rho$. The high-order energy differential inequality in [F6], integrated from the initial slice and using this lower bound, gives one finite bound $M=M(R_0,\rho,T)$ for $\|u(t)\|_{H^s}$ throughout every such interval of existence; it continues to hold across uniqueness-glued restarts because the solution and its energy agree at each join. Choose $R_*>M$. Let $K_{\rm mid}$ be the closed state-space tube of radius $d/3$ about the reference range; it is compact and contained in $\operatorname{int}K_1$. Since the coefficient time interval is open and contains compact $J$, choose $\tau_0>0$ so every translate centered at $t_0\in J$ is defined on $[-\tau_0,\tau_0]$. On the resulting compact time-state set, all coefficient bounds used in the Galerkin proof of [F5] are uniform and $A^0\ge aI$. Apply that proof to each translated family $A^\mu(t_0+\sigma,x,z),B(t_0+\sigma,x,z)$ with input set $K_{\rm mid}$, output set $K_1$ and norm radius $R_*$. The common coefficient bounds, state margin and radius give one local time $\tau_*>0$, decreased if necessary so $\tau_*\le\tau_0$, and one solution bound $M_{\rm loc}$ independent of $t_0$. Smooth persistence [F6] gives smooth local solutions for the smooth restart data. [given, F5, F6, algebra]

Fix the comparison constant in step 3.3 using the bounds $R_*$ and the corresponding time-derivative bound supplied by the unforced equation, [F3] and [F4]. Choose the initial $H^s$ radius so small that this estimate keeps $\|u-\bar u\|_{C(J;H^r)}<\min\{1,d/(4C_{\rm emb})\}$, where $C_{\rm emb}$ is the embedding constant from [F7]. On every partial interval of existence, a first exit from either bootstrap bound is impossible: the strict estimate persists there, the state range lies in $K_{\rm mid}$, and step 4.1 bounds the $H^s$ norm strictly below $R_*$. If a constructed interval ends before $T$, its endpoint data therefore lie in $K_{\rm mid}$ with $H^s$ norm below $R_*$. Step 4.1 supplies a restarted solution on a time interval centered there, with $H^s$ norm at most $M_{\rm loc}$; the previous and restarted solutions overlap to the left of the restart time. Uniqueness [F2], applied with the common bound $\max\{R_*,M_{\rm loc}\}$, identifies them on that overlap. The same bootstrap bounds then continue on the restarted interval. Since $\tau_*>0$ is independent of the restart point, finitely many such restarts cover $J$. This proves the claimed neighborhood. [step 3.3, step 4.1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

For the fixed harmonic-gauge reduction in the geometric clause, let $H$ be its gauge residual and $E$ its Einstein residual. Define $P\subseteq[0,T]$ to consist of times at which $H=0$ and the normal Einstein constraints vanish on the whole slice $\{t\}\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$. The given initial gauge condition and constraints put $0$ in $P$. At any $t_0\in P$, the reduced matter solution has conserved stress by the stated fixed-model hypotheses, so [F13] gives an open neighborhood of that entire slice on which $H=0$ and $E=0$. The torus slice is compact, hence this neighborhood contains all slices with $|t-t_0|<\varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon>0$; thus $P$ is relatively open. If $t_n\in P$ converges to $t_0$, smoothness of the reduced metric, matter fields and their residuals makes $H=0$ and the normal constraint residuals zero at $t_0$, so $P$ is closed. At an endpoint use [F5] to extend the smooth reduced solution a short distance, and [F2] to identify it with the original solution on the overlap; this makes the same open-set argument valid there. Since $[0,T]$ is connected, $P=[0,T]$. The neighborhoods from [F13] therefore cover the slab, proving the original Einstein-matter equations throughout it. [given, step 4.2, A1, F2, F5, F8, F12, F13, algebra]

For each radial path, [F3] and the ODE give $(Q^{\mathsf T}\eta Q)'=0$, hence $Q(q)^{\mathsf T}\eta Q(q)=\eta$ and $Q(q)$ is invertible. The finite curvilinear-triangle subdivision is a finite connected CW complex $K$; choose the lower-left corner as basepoint and a maximal tree in its one-skeleton. By [F7], $\pi_1(K)$ has generators given by non-tree edge loops closed along the tree and relators given by based triangular face boundaries. old_steps: For each point $p$, use [F1] to choose a neighborhood $U$ and a smooth future-directed tetrad $E$ there. If that sign is negative, replace $E_1$ by $-E_1$. This preserves orthonormality and the future direction of $E_0$ and makes $E$ positively oriented by [F2]. Thus positively oriented future tetrads exist locally. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

Let $u,v$ lie in a common fiber of $P^+_g(M)$. Since $u$ is an isomorphism, $A:=u^{-1}v$ is the unique real matrix with $v=u\circ A$. The isometry condition gives $A^{\mathsf T}\eta A=\eta$. Positivity of the two frame orientations gives $\det A>0$, while the Lorentz identity gives $\det A=\pm1$, hence $\det A=1$. Because $u(e_0)$ and $v(e_0)$ are future timelike, $A e_0$ is future timelike; so $A$ preserves the selected future component and belongs to $SO^+(1,3)$. This proves that the right action is transitive on each fiber; uniqueness of $A$ proves freeness. [given, F3, algebra]

For a local positively oriented future tetrad section $E$ on $U$, define $\Psi_E:U\times SO^+(1,3)\to(P^+_g(M))|_U$ by $\Psi_E(p,A)=E(p)\circ A$. Step 2.1 makes this map bijective. Its inverse sends a frame $u$ over $p$ to $(p,E(p)^{-1}\circ u)$; the matrix entries of this second component are smooth because they are obtained by applying the smooth dual coframe of $E$ to the smooth frame vectors of $u$. Thus $\Psi_E$ is a smooth local product chart. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F4, algebra]

If $E'$ is another such section on an overlap, write $E'(p)=E(p)\circ A(p)$. The transition between the charts is $(p,B)\mapsto(p,A(p)B)$, which is smooth; its inverse $(p,B)\mapsto(p,A(p)^{-1}B)$ is smooth because inversion is smooth in the Lie group of [F4]. The right action is smooth in these charts and the projection is the product projection. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F4, algebra]

The charts of step 3.1 and smooth transitions from step 4.1 give $P^+_g(M)$ local products $U\times SO^+(1,3)$. For second countability, let $\mathcal B$ be a countable base of $M$; for each $B\in\mathcal B$ contained in at least one local-section neighborhood, use [A1] to select one such neighborhood. The selected countable family covers $M$, and countable bases of each selected $U\times SO^+(1,3)$ give a countable base of the total space by [F4,F6]. Thus the local charts define a smooth manifold structure. Freeness and fiberwise transitivity were proved in step 2.1; by [F5], this is a smooth right principal $SO^+(1,3)$-bundle. old_steps: For each dual factor, choose an orthonormal basis of $V_e$ and use its dual-basis inner product; this is basis-independent because a change between orthonormal bases preserves the Euclidean coefficient norm. The matrix of the dual action is the transpose of the inverse unitary matrix, hence is unitary. Tensor products of orthonormal bases are an orthonormal basis for the displayed tensor inner product, so the diagonal action is unitary by [F3]–[F4]. Its matrix entries are finite sums and products of continuous entries of the edge representations, so [F7] makes $R_v$ strongly continuous. [given, F3, F4, F7, algebra]

For fixed $w\in W_v$, define $T_w:\mathbb C\to W_v$ by $T_w(z)=zw$, with the trivial representation on $\mathbb C$. It is linear and bounded by [F8], with $\|T_w\|=\|w\|$. The intertwining equation $T_w(z)=R_v(g)T_w(z)$ for all $z$ is equivalent to $w\in W_v^{SU(2)}$. [given, F6, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

By [F1], $SU(2)$ is compact Hausdorff; by [F2] and [F5], its normalized Haar probability exists under the stated full AC assumption. The hypotheses of [F9]–[F10] now hold for $H=\mathbb C$, $J=W_v$, and $T=T_w$, using [F6], [F7], and steps 1.1–1.2. Since the trivial representation acts as the identity, the weak Haar average of $T_w$ is $T_{P_vw}$, where the finite-dimensional vector integral is defined coordinatewise. The range clause of [F10] therefore gives $P_v^2=P_v$, $\|P_v\|\le1$, and $\operatorname{ran}P_v=W_v^{SU(2)}$. [given, F1, F2, F5, F6, F7, F9, F10, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

If $x\in\operatorname{ran}P_v$ and $y\in\ker P_v$, then $P_v(x+ty)=x$ for every complex scalar $t$. Contractivity gives $\|x\|\le\|x+ty\|$. Squaring and taking real $t$ of both signs forces $\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle=0$; taking $t$ purely imaginary of both signs forces $\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle=0$. Hence range and kernel are orthogonal. Since an idempotent has $W_v=\operatorname{ran}P_v\oplus\ker P_v$, $P_v$ is the orthogonal projection onto its invariant range. [given, F10, step 1.3, algebra]

On $W=\bigotimes_vW_v$, each vertex operator acts as $P_v$ on one factor and identity on the others. Operators on distinct tensor factors commute, so their product is an idempotent whose range is $\bigotimes_v\operatorname{ran}P_v$, the tensors invariant under every vertex action. It is the orthogonal projection onto this joint invariant subspace because tensor products of orthogonal projections are orthogonal projections in the product Hilbert structure. If the graph has no vertices, the empty product is the identity on $\mathbb C$, consistent with the statement. [given, F3, F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
